title: Getting Started With Habeas Petitions: An Interview With Christine Zeller-Powell
description:
These ICE detentions were different.
So that was when we started doing habeas work.
There is incredible pressure of people in U.S. immigration detention to self-deport.
Q: How do you balance habeas work with other programmatic work?
A: There’s certainly other work to be done outside of our habeas work!
text:
CLINIC sat down with Christine Zeller-Powell, director of the Refugee and Immigrant Services Program at Catholic Community Services in Eugene, Oregon, to discuss how her program began filing habeas corpus petitions in federal court in response to the illegal detentions of their clients they observed.

Q: Can you please share with me what your role is and how long you have been doing this work?

A: My name is Christine Zeller-Powell and I am an attorney who serves as the director of the Refugee and Immigrant Services Program (RISP). I’ve been in the work of immigration legal services for about 10 years, including helping start our refugee resettlement system back in 2016, in response to the Syrian refugee crisis.

Our work resettling refugees abruptly stopped in 2017, under the first Trump administration, so we pivoted to providing services to asylum seekers who arriving from the border. We’ve been expanding our legal and social services since then.

Q: How has your work changed in the last year or so?

A: Well, the immediate impact of the second Trump administration for us was that we stopped seeing new arrivals of asylum seekers and refugees, and serving new arrivals had been our primary focus before.

We started to see detentions of community members while they were attending regular check-ins at our local ICE office. In the past, we hadn’t seen people detained at ICE check-ins unless there were serious criminal issues. These ICE detentions were different. They were arresting people who were complying or trying to comply with the immigration processes and didn’t have any criminal charges or arrests. These detentions didn’t seem like lawful arrests and they turned out to involve due process violations. So that was when we started doing habeas work.

Q: Can you give me an example of what you mean by unlawful detentions based on due process violations?

A: Sure. One of our first habeas cases involved a community member with a pending asylum application whom ICE detained because ICE said they changed their address without telling them, which turned out not to be true.

Another of our first cases involved a man with a pending asylum application who had an order of release from detention. In some orders of release, there is a condition stated in the release that you can’t travel outside the state for more than 48 hours without telling ICE. But this man did not have that condition as part of his release agreement. He traveled outside the state for work and was very communicative with ICE the whole time. He came back and was suddenly arrested. When we brought it to court, it turned out ICE had arrested him for traveling outside of the state for more than 48 hours, even though that wasn’t actually a condition of his order of release.

In these situations, these people would have been detained and likely deported. There is incredible pressure of people in U.S. immigration detention to self-deport. For people who don’t self-deport, their cases are heard from detention, where it is much harder to gather evidence and prepare for a hearing, access to counsel is restricted, and outcomes are much worse for people. All because ICE arrested them on illegal grounds, yanking the rug out from under them when they were complying with the law, and then held them in detention.

Q: How did you get started filing these cases?

A: Well, we had never filed cases in federal court before. Most immigration attorneys don’t need to do that kind of work. So, we knew we needed help and we started putting out feelers for co-counsel who could partner with us.

We came across a group of public defenders who were eager to do this kind of work. We had the connections to the immigrant clients and the rapid response network which could help us identify the appropriate cases; they had the experience in federal court but lacked immigration experience. It was a great partnership.

With their help, we created our case templates and studied the process. We told them we were ready to start when they were. The very next day, a case came up, and we acted fast.

Q: Why do you have to take action so quickly in these cases?

A: Well, Oregon is unique in that we do not have an overnight detention facility. If a community member is arrested and detained by ICE, they transfer him/her out of state, to Tacoma, Washington. If we can file a habeas case within hours of the detention, we can prevent this transfer so that the case can remain in our jurisdiction, with Oregon judges, etc. If not, we will have to partner with attorneys in Washington and it becomes a lot more complicated. So, these cases require us to drop everything to file them immediately.

We have a really good relationship with our local rapid response network, so when we hear of a detention, we can usually move very quickly to talk to the family members and/or eyewitnesses and decide whether to file.

Q: How do you balance habeas work with other programmatic work?

A: There’s certainly other work to be done outside of our habeas work! We continue to prepare and file applications with USCIS and EOIR. When our public defender co-counsels ran out of capacity for a time, we tried to take on the habeas work ourselves, but it was just too much on top of already managing our program. But we’ve since developed other partnerships, and now we’re working to help other attorneys, often volunteers, get equipped to do this work as well so that the load can be lightened. We invite them to be co-counsel with us so they can learn the ropes for habeas litigation.

Q: Why do you do this work and what keeps you going with things are challenging?

text:
Generating Resistance

The daily onslaught of new immigration policies and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s (ICE’s) enforcement is head-spinning. Heavily armed, masked agents brutally arresting Spanish-speaking individuals at construction sites and parking lots has become commonplace. Individuals have been removed to countries like South Sudan and Uganda, despite having no ties to those countries. ICE has implemented surges of enforcement in cities like Los Angeles, Chicago, and Portland. And of course, the enforcement surge in Minneapolis led to mass protests even before the ICE killings of two U.S. citizens—Renee Good and Alex Pretti.

Resistance to the Trump 2.0 ICE Age has been waged from a range of sectors. Musicians, artists, social media influencers, and everyday people with no history of protesting have been motivated to engage. From neighbors helping migrant families walk their children to school to religious leaders offering places of reflection, and Japanese Americans who see the parallels between World War II internment and ICE detention, the level and intensity of resistance are striking.

The legal community is stepping up big time with legal services and pro bono attorneys taking on an overwhelming number of cases—not just in removal proceedings but also seeking habeas relief in federal district courts. Impact litigation led by groups like the American Civil Liberties Union is also vitally important. Strikingly, federal district court judges are repeatedly issuing rulings that are highly critical of the administration and U.S. Department of Justice attorneys for their disregard of previous orders.

The Necessity of Resistance

The inhumanity, overreach, and constant attacks on basic rights in the Trump 2.0 ICE Age demand that anyone with a sense of justice and decency stand up and voice opposition. The Trump playbook is clear: Implement an authoritarian regime with absolute control and suppress opposition by imposing intense restrictions through overt tyranny to maintain power. Thus, Trump and his closest advisors malign judges who rule against them and label reporters as proponents of “fake news” for simply asking straightforward questions.

As Trump entered the second year of his second term, his behavior was more authoritarian than ever, overthrowing the Venezuelan government, launching a virtual siege of Minneapolis, declaring he would take control of Greenland, trying to force Federal Reserve Chair Jerome Powell to resign, and launching an unprovoked war on Iran. To political scientists, Trump’s actions are worrisome violations of core democratic norms and values and not simply partisan and ideological disagreements with Democrats and the left. Democratic Senators Elissa Slotkin and Mark Kelly are being investigated for organizing and appearing in a video imploring military service members to refuse “illegal orders.” This is reminiscent of dictatorships around the world, causing them to regard Trump as “an existential threat to democracy.”

The lessons from Timothy Snyder’s book On Tyranny are quite relevant. By analyzing 20th-century Europe to identify conditions that enabled established democracies to transform into dictatorships, Snyder warns of America’s turn toward authoritarianism. Before the general elections in November 2024, Snyder noted that On Tyranny was written in a defensive mode and that if its lessons are heeded and implemented, things could get much better in 2025 for those who want to maintain democracy and the rule of law in the United States. With Trump elected for a second time, things got much worse in 2025.

Snyder’s historical lesson teaches us that resistance is important in the face of authoritarianism and tyranny; authoritarian systems depend on obedience, fear, and silence to survive. Resistance is also an exercise of, as well as a method to protect, human dignity and to preserve freedom. Resistance asserts that these rights, such as speech and assembly, are inherent, not gifts from the state, and that they cannot be legitimately revoked at will. Resistance is a statement of opposition to the concentration of unchecked power as well as a demonstration that those who desire unchecked power are failing. As such, resistance challenges the authoritarian’s foundations of obedience, fear, and silence and keeps open the possibility of freedom, accountability, and truth.

Honestly, resistance today is also necessary in the context of a president whose mental competence and stability have been called into question. Consider arenas far beyond immigration. His acts of war against Venezuela and Iran have been deemed illegal by many, and he has been called “completely insane” after sharing a post declaring himself “Acting President of Venezuela.” His plan to take control of Greenland was labeled “blackmail” and an exercise of “unilateralism.”

Mental health professionals link Trump’s behavior to symptoms of “narcissistic personality disorder, characterized by self-centeredness and a lack of empathy for others.” They have described Trump’s mental state as “indicative of psychopathic personality disorder, which includes a lack of guilt or shame, extreme impulsiveness, and a desire to control others.” They claim that Trump displays “extraordinary grandiosity and a minimal tendency to compromise.”

Trump’s psychological problems are presumed to be so bad that a number of lawmakers called for the 25th Amendment to be invoked after he told Norway’s prime minister that his position on purchasing or taking over Greenland is tied to not winning the Nobel Peace Prize, and he no longer feels obligated to “think purely of Peace.” Lawmakers contend that Trump is “mentally ill . . . putting all of our lives at risk” and is “unfit to lead and clearly out of control.” Section 4 of the 25th Amendment concerns the removal of a president who is unable or unwilling to perform their duties. If the president is incapable of serving but does not voluntarily transfer power, they can be declared unable to hold the position by the vice president, along with a “majority of either the principal officers of the executive departments or of such other body as Congress may by law provide.”

The president’s staffing in his second term adds further concern. In his first term, those surrounding Trump justified working in his administration, saying they would serve as guardrails against his most extreme impulses. People who sought to restrain the president then, like former chief of staff John Kelly and White House counsel Donald McGahn II, are no longer serving in this administration. We are now seeing how a “truly unshackled Trump” wields his power. In the absence of guardrails to control a mentally imbalanced authoritarian, we need resistance to create friction—legal, social, economic, or political—to slow or weaken his control.

The day-to-day challenges presented by Trump’s head-spinning anti-immigrant agenda can be exhausting and demoralizing. We need to constantly remind ourselves that authoritarianism thrives when people believe resistance is futile or dangerous. Even small acts of dissent can break the illusion of total control and show others they are not alone. We must resist and confront each and every tyrannical element of the Trump-Vance authoritarian regime. Ruling against the administration’s attempt to require California to turn over the personal information of millions of voters, Judge David Carter of the U.S. District Court for the Central District of California reminds us that “[t]he taking of democracy does not occur in one fell swoop; it is chipped away piece-by-piece until there is nothing left.” We need to defend each precious piece of democracy.

Multiple creative examples of resisters surround us—lawyers, religious leaders, journalists, artists, musicians, and politicians, but they are mostly regular people at No Kings marches and countless demonstrations. They are inspirational, challenging authoritarianism by keeping justice and human worth alive under the most anti- immigrant administration of our lifetimes.

title: An Illusion of Choice: Rights Without Resources Are Not Freedom or Justice
description:
The legal community understands better than most that rights without resources and power are paper promises—not freedom, not justice.
Political and civil rights without economic rights are not merely inadequate; they are a co-optation of the very ideas of freedom, justice, and rights.
Indeed, choice is an illusion when one lacks the power and resources to exercise it.
The Economic Rights Component of Human Rights That We Abandoned More than 75 years ago, in the aftermath of the atrocities of World War II, Eleanor Roosevelt led a coalition of global leaders to establish the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR)—codifying freedom across five categories: civil rights, political rights, social rights, cultural rights, and economic rights.
We have grossly scaled back our commitments to this covenant, especially in the domain of economic rights.
text:
The legal community understands better than most that rights without resources and power are paper promises—not freedom, not justice. The right to vote when you are hungry is not freedom. The right to protest when you are unhoused is not justice. Political and civil rights without economic rights are not merely inadequate; they are a co-optation of the very ideas of freedom, justice, and rights. Indeed, choice is an illusion when one lacks the power and resources to exercise it.

The Economic Rights Component of Human Rights That We Abandoned

More than 75 years ago, in the aftermath of the atrocities of World War II, Eleanor Roosevelt led a coalition of global leaders to establish the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR)—codifying freedom across five categories: civil rights, political rights, social rights, cultural rights, and economic rights. We have grossly scaled back our commitments to this covenant, especially in the domain of economic rights. Our contemporary political economic consensus has worked hard to sever what the UDHR understood as inseparable—that authentic civil, social, and political freedoms do not exist without economic rights. Freedom was never simply the protection of property in the absence of economic security. That narrowed interpretation is designed to serve, not the masses, but the interests of the wealthy, whose share of capital continues to accumulate and exclude others. Material resources are a necessary precondition for economic agency—and for a fully human life.

Beginning in the 1970s, a neoliberal paradigm dismantled that vision—juxtaposing a false dichotomy of market versus government intervention, prioritizing property rights over human rights, and degrading investments in human capacities by racializing them as government handouts to undeserving and defective people. The consequences of those choices have been written into the fabric of our political economy and distribution. For instance, over the past four decades, the bottom half of Americans have seen negligible gains in their wealth, while the top 1 percent have experienced increases exceeding 500 percent. Half the country holds less than 2 percent of its total wealth. These gross disparities, which certainly are not limited to wealth, are not simply happenstance. Rather, these outcomes are the predictable results of deliberate policies: the deregulation of financial markets, the erosion of labor power, the defunding of public investment, and the steady corporate consolidation of major institutions— media, banking, communications—that is itself antidemocratic. It is naive, at best, to ignore how easily economic might has translated into political might.

An Economic “Rights” Way Forward: Empower People as the Point, Purpose, and Mechanism for a Fair, Just, and Thriving Economy

Our public infrastructure should first and foremost serve and invest in its people. When properly resourced, people are innovative and productive agents who make dynamic contributions that benefit themselves, the communities in which they live, and the broader economy.

Wherever one falls on the spectrum between capitalism and socialism, do not lose sight of the point: People are the purpose of our economy. And as the UDHR made clear, the role of government is to ensure that our children, families, and workers have adequate access to the quantity and quality of economic resources necessary to thrive, not merely to survive. This is the concept of economic rights. And in the 21st century, these resources should affirmatively include housing, health care, banking and financial services, reproductive autonomy and agency in family formation, the right to unionize and collectively bargain, basic income, good jobs, a capital foundation, quality education from grade school through college, and the freedom to move through society without the threat of detention or bodily harm from state-sanctioned terror because one’s identity is linked to a stigmatized group. Recognizing them as such will correct the historical inadequacies of the human rights agenda.

These rights should be designed, managed, and implemented in ways that are affirmatively (i.e., intentionally) inclusive of all social identity groups. Without that intentionality, the default will be exclusion. Indeed, America has a long history of exclusion and discrimination on the basis of social identity. Indeed, President Franklin D. Roosevelt’s well-documented Faustian Bargain with Southern Democrats to advance his New Deal agenda was designed to leave intact a Jim Crow apartheid-like structure that largely excluded Black Americans and Black-led institutions from the full public investments that many credit as seeding the American middle class.

With sad irony, this Faustian Bargain, which effectively solidified Black Americans as an economic underclass, may have also helped facilitate the race-based political fodder, such as castigating social welfare programs with coded racial language as wasteful spending to irresponsible “welfare queens” and “deadbeat dads,” and which ultimately fueled the neoliberal backlash to the human rights movements in the first place.

Investing in human capacities—what Nobel Laureate Amartya Sen called the capabilities approach—promotes inclusion, empowers people against predation, global pandemics, economic volatility, and affordability crises while generating the positive externalities and productive macroeconomic multipliers that strengthen our economy as a whole. This is how economic security produces substantive rights and authentic freedom.

text:
“In my district, and all across the state, immigrants are being subjected to a life filled with fear and anxiety like never before – they are scared to attend their healthcare appointments, go to work, go grocery shopping, go to school and to seek justice in our court systems or police departments,” said Senator Sal N. DiDomenico. “This is not how you create a vibrant and prosperous state, and I am proud to work alongside Congresswoman Pressley and our Chelsea leaders to restore faith in government and peace in our communities. I want to thank Congresswoman Pressley and La Colaborativa for hosting this essential community forum to give voice and space to our neighbors who have had their rights stripped away by the federal government. We are fortunate to have Congresswoman Pressley push forward each day and continue fighting against the hatred and division that is coming from the White House.”

“When families come to us facing some of the most difficult immigration challenges, they need more than sympathy. They need action. Congresswoman Pressley and her team have consistently been there to help resolve complex cases and deliver answers for families when they matter most.” – State Representative Judith Garcia

“We hold deep gratitude for the community members, comrades, Congresswoman Pressley, and her team for creating space to share stories, lessons, and strategies. We are especially grateful to our comrades at Delaney Hall who organized the recent hunger strike. At a time when many feel discouraged, they chose to organize, resist, and make their voices heard. The lesson from Delaney Hall is bigger than any single facility. There is no such thing as a humane detention center. From Delaney Hall to Pike County Jail, Wyatt Detention Center, Eloy Detention Center, and Plymouth County Correctional Facility, the call must be the same: close them all. Our communities have power. text:
As we enter the heart of opinion season, we thought it would be helpful to revisit past Closer Looks on how SCOTUSblog covers opinion announcements. This piece was originally published on March 31.

If you regularly attend our opinion day live blogs, you’ve likely noticed that certain questions come up nearly every time. For example, do we know in advance which opinions are coming? (No.) Is live audio available from the courtroom during opinion announcements? (Also no.) And how many boxes are there? (It varies.)

The box question typically sparks a series of additional questions from blog newcomers and veterans alike. What are these boxes you’re speaking of? Why do they matter? And, more recently, do the boxes seem heavy or light?

Let us take those questions in order. First off, the boxes are literal boxes. They are made of light blue carboard and look something like this. The boxes are used by the Supreme Court’s Public Information Office to bring copies of soon-to-be-released opinions to members of the press. A member of the PIO team lifts them onto desks in the PIO’s outer office at 9:55 a.m. EDT, when the five-minute buzzer sounds. That means that, although reporters do not see the actual opinions before they are announced by the court shortly after 10:00 a.m. EDT, they do see the box(es) before then (which Amy reports on the live blog), prompting the box count discussion.

As to the second question, the box count is significant because it gives us a sense of how many opinions might be coming. If there is just one box, the court is unlikely to be releasing more than three short opinions – and, indeed, is likely only releasing one or two opinions – because copies of three long opinions wouldn’t fit in a single box. It follows that when there are two boxes, we can safely predict that at least three opinions are on the way.

In recent live blogs, we’ve also talked – it may be more accurate to say joked – about how heavy or “puffy” the day’s box seems to be. Amy describes whether it seemed to take more effort than usual for the box to be carried in. Much like the box count seeks to estimate how many opinions may be released, this metric is aimed at making a more educated guess about how many opinions a box contains.

Admittedly, tracking the box count (and box weight) only gets you so far on opinion days. Sure, learning that there are two or three boxes instead of one makes it clear that it will be a busy morning, but knowing the box count on Friday, Feb. 20 (one) didn’t mean we knew for sure that the tariffs decision was coming. The reporters at the court got that answer when Chief Justice John Roberts began announcing the tariffs ruling in the courtroom, which prompted staffers in the Public Information Office to hand out copies of the opinion to those gathered around the box.

Still, this tracking can bring a sense of control to chaotic opinion days, and, perhaps most importantly, it’s a fun aspect of one very serious institution.

authors: MIKE CERULLO, NBC 10 NEWS, MIKE CERULLO
description:

(WJAR) In May, the court appointed a special counsel to investigate the possibility of misconduct by Assistant U.S. Attorney Kevin Bolan.

text:
The U.S. District Court for Rhode Island has raised the possibility that Immigration and Customs Enforcement officials deliberately “set up” a federal judge so that it could make a false attack on her, which put her in personal danger.

Chief Judge John McConnell also issued a harshly critical letter to an assistant U.S. Attorney, but stopped short of formal disciplinary proceedings.

Mike Cerullo reports on the case of a judge potentially being "set up" by ICE officials. (WJAR)

In May, the court appointed a special counsel to investigate the possibility of misconduct by Assistant U.S. Attorney Kevin Bolan. Bolan admitted that he had not the judge all the necessary information before she released a man from ICE custody.

The man was wanted for homicide in the Dominican Republic, but prosecutors never disclosed that to Judge Melissa DuBose.

After the release of Bryan Rafael Gomez, the Department of Homeland Security issued a press release and social media posts condemning her as an activist judge. The press release remains active on the DHS website.

MORE: Federal government apologizes to Rhode Island judge over release of detainee

The Special Counsel released its finding Tuesday, describing “some deeply troubling circumstances”

The counsel’s report noted that the government’s response to Gomez’s request for release “deliberately did not disclose that Mr. Gomez faced awarrant related to alleged homicide.”

It also noted that the DHS press release singled out “Judge DuBose by name, criticizing her ruling and falsely suggesting that she knowingly ‘released a violent criminal illegal alien who is wanted for murder in the Dominican Republic.’”

The report continued, “This troubling sequence raised the question whether ICE deliberately manipulated the case briefing on the Gómez petition to set up Judge DuBose to release Mr. Gómez so that it could make a false attack against her. False statements by government officials, as exemplified in ICE’s April 30 press release, are unacceptable – they undermine public trust in government; impair judicial decision-making; interfere with the rule of law, and as we have seen, have real world consequences.”

In his letter to Bolan, Judge McConnell said the special counsel’s report found “sufficient evidence to conclude that your conduct on the Gomez case violated the duty of candor you ow the Court.”

MORE: Rhode Island judge considers whether to hold government in contempt over man's release

In a subsequent hearing, Judge DuBose ordered Gomez be detained by ICE, but Gomez has not been taken back into custody.

"I think the court finds it extremely troubling that ICE withheld information from a judge, directed their attorney not to share that information and then turned around and publicly scrutinized her," said NBC 10 Legal Analyst Austin Dana.

Dana read through McConnell's cautionary letter to Bolan.

"What the court is saying in the letter to Attorney Bolan is, you should have asked for more time, or you should've brought this up the chain of command and gotten permission to give the judge the information that she needed," Dana said.

The Department of Homeland Security is standing by its attack on Judge DuBose, which remains publicly available. The agency's only statement to NBC 10 Tuesday was an op-ed written more than one month ago, calling the ICE press release, "factually true," despite Bolan's statement last month in federal court calling the post, "inaccurate."

A spokesperson for DuBose and McConnell declined to comment.

NBC 10 reached out to Bolan, but did not immediately hear back.

text:
Detainees from Florida’s notorious “Alligator Alcatraz” immigration jail have been relocated to other facilities, according to US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

The detention facility in the remote Everglades, celebrated by Donald Trump for its harsh conditions, has been widely expected to close. It quickly attracted headlines for the brutal treatment of detainees after opening last year.

ICE announced on Tuesday that all detainees at the state-run site had been moved, but did not specify how many, or where they were taken.

The agency, NBC Miami reported, said: “As we enter into hurricane season, ICE and the state of Florida have moved illegal aliens from the soft sided facility. For the safety of the illegal alien detainees, we transferred them to other facilities.”

ICE did not immediately respond when contacted for comment by the Guardian.

The transfers come amid allegations of human rights abuses at the detention center. In a report published in December 2025, Amnesty International alleged that detainees were shackled inside a 2ft-high metal cage and left outdoors without water for extended periods.

According to the report, the cage was used as a form of arbitrary punishment. One detainee told Amnesty International: “One time, two people in my cell were calling out to the guards telling them that I needed my medication. Ten guards rushed into the cell and threw them to the ground. They were taken to the ‘box’ and punished just for trying to help me. I saw a guy who was put in it for an entire day.”

The jail, which opened in July 2025, costs Florida taxpayers an estimated $1.2m a day to operate, according to an investigation by the Florida Tributary.

In May, the New York Times reported that Florida plans to shut down the facility. Citing a federal official and three people familiar with the matter, the outlet said state officials told vendors that detainees would be transferred out at the beginning of June.

Speaking at a press conference last month, Florida governor Ron DeSantis said the state “didn’t build any permanent facilities down there, because we knew it was going to be temporary”, but did not provide a timeline for the closure.

Meanwhile, a Guardian report published earlier this month found that more than half a dozen detainees alleged they were given “rotten” water containing mosquito larvae. According to the detainees, prison guards used the allegedly spoiled water to pressure them into signing documents written in English that they could not understand.

text:
A group of Haitian citizens who are beneficiaries of a program that allows them to stay in the United States came to the Supreme Court on Tuesday, asking the justices to throw out a dispute over whether the Trump administration can end the program, known as Temporary Protected Status, for Haiti. The justices heard oral arguments in the case in late April, but the Haitian citizens told the court on Tuesday that it should toss the case without deciding it – a procedure known as “dismiss as improvidently granted” – based on “newly discovered facts [that] bear directly on the merits of” their claims. In particular, the Haitians contended, a July 1 notice by then-Secretary of Homeland Security Kristi Noem of her intent to end the TPS program for Haiti “relied on a knowingly false statement.”

Congress enacted the Temporary Protected Status program in 1990. The program gives the Department of Homeland Security the power to designate a country’s citizens as eligible to remain in the U.S. and work if they cannot return safely to their own country because of a natural disaster, armed conflict, or other “extraordinary and temporary” conditions there. In 2010, shortly after a powerful earthquake struck the country, causing extensive damage and hundreds of thousands of deaths, Janet Napolitano – then the DHS secretary – designated Haiti under the TPS program. The designation initially lasted for 18 months but was repeatedly re-extended until 2025.

After Noem announced that the Trump administration planned to end Haiti’s TPS designation, a group of Haitian nationals in the United States went to federal court in Washington, D.C., where they argued both that the decision to end the TPS designation violated the federal law governing administrative agencies and that it violated the Constitution because it was intended to discriminate against them based on their race.

The lower courts ruled in favor of the Haitian nationals and barred the government from ending the program while their challenge continued. The Trump administration then went to the Supreme Court, asking the justices to pause both that ruling and a similar one in favor of Syrian nationals. The justices temporarily left the lower court orders in place, but they agreed to take up both cases and heard arguments on April 29.

The Haitian nationals on Tuesday asked the justices to dismiss their case without ruling on it, pointing to “new facts” that they said show that “the termination of Haiti’s TPS designation was a preordained outcome motivated by discriminatory” intent. They told the justices that they had obtained new documents from the government indicating that Noem’s July 1 notice terminating the TPS program for Haiti “relied on a knowingly false statement—namely, the assertion that” Noem “had consulted with the Department of State when in fact she had not.” Moreover, they added, the documents show that the July 1 notice “was based on an unprecedented rationale” for ending Haiti’s TPS status – the U.S. national interest – and was “published only after a political appointee issued an unusual eleventh-hour verbal directive instructing career officials to abandon their recommendation that Haiti’s TPS designation be extended.” These additional facts could, if true, bolster the Haitian nationals’ argument that Noem’s decision to end the TPS program for Haiti had not complied with the federal law governing administrative agencies – for example, because Noem had not followed the procedures required by law and because she had not provided an adequate explanation for her decision.

Because the facts of the case continue to unfold, the Haitian nationals argued, the court should not now decide whether they “are likely to succeed on the merits of their claims.” Instead, they wrote, the court should send the case back so that the lower courts can issue a final decision on the merits after all of the fact-finding has been completed.

The motion to dismiss the case applies only to the challenge by Haitian nationals; even if the court were to grant it, it would not necessarily affect the justices’ ability to rule on the case involving Syrian nationals.

text:
Sign up for Chalkbeat Chicago’s free daily newsletter to keep up with the latest news on Chicago Public Schools.

An Illinois congressman is seeking to expand support for immigrant students in schools — a move that builds on protections state lawmakers approved last year.

U.S. Rep. Jesús “Chuy” Garcia, who represents several Latino communities in Chicago, introduced legislation Tuesday that would provide federal support to schools serving students affected by immigration enforcement. Joined by Chicago Board of Education member Yesenia Lopez and Latino Policy Forum President Linda Xóchitl Tortolero, Garcia unveiled the proposal, dubbed The Right to Learn Act, Tuesday before more than 30 students and staff at Richard J. Daley College in south Chicago.

“For immigrant kids, school is often the first place that they have in this country. They feel welcome, they feel seen, and they feel heard,” Garcia said. “Too many students now walk through the same doors in fear.”

But passing the bill will be a tall order in the Republican-controlled House for Garcia and the cohort of largely progressive House Democrats who co-sponsored it, including Minnesota Rep. Ilhan Omar. That could change if Democrats flip the chamber in November’s midterms.

The bill would create a federal grant program for schools impacted by immigration enforcement. Schools could use the funding to hire bilingual counselors and social workers, promote trauma-informed and culturally sensitive mental health services, and provide emergency assistance to families in need. The U.S. Department of Education would administer the program.

The proposal comes as the Trump administration seeks to reduce educational funding for programs serving undocumented and immigrant students. Some of those efforts were carried out through President Donald Trump’s executive orders, including one targeting states that provide in-state tuition for undocumented college students.

Federal agencies have also played a role in cutting back services for immigrant children. Last year, the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services barred undocumented children from using Head Start, a federal preschool program aimed at supporting low-income families. That policy is held up in a legal battle, but its looming implementation has worried some parents.

As the Education Department continues to wind down its services and transfer programs to other agencies, the Office of English Language Acquisition has been dissolved. Its funding for English language learning and teacher training is being folded into other programs, according to Education Department officials in April.

Garcia says his legislation contains the “spirit of that office,” adding that federal services such as the Office of English Language Acquisition helped ensure mental health support for students is “culturally rooted and considered.”

Given federal rollbacks and Trump’s mass deportation campaign, Illinois state lawmakers took steps last year to enhance protections for immigrant children.

A new state law requires Illinois schools to follow policies on how to respond to immigration enforcement agents on campus and prohibits schools from requesting a student’s immigration status or Social Security number. Another law passed last year largely blocks university and childcare staff from revealing a family’s immigration status.

Garcia’s bill is a way to extend those protections at the federal level, said state Rep. Edgar Gonzalez, who represents Little Village and Brighton Park, during the press conference.

“You need to put your money where your mouth is, and a bill like this really allows for our schools to make sure they’re safe spaces,” he said.

text:
Today, Congresswoman Veronica Escobar (TX-16) joined Rep. Lloyd Doggett, every other member of the Texas Democratic Delegation in the U.S. House of Representatives, and five other Representatives in urging the Department of Homeland Security to rescind the environmental and historic preservation waivers granted at Big Bend. These waivers were granted by the Trump administration to bypass federal environmental laws in order to speed up work on border barriers in the area.

This letter comes after Congresswoman Escobar spoke in support of an amendment last week during the House Appropriations Committee mark up of the Fiscal Year 2027 Homeland Security Bill. The amendment was to prohibit the construction of a barrier or wall at Big Bend. It was rejected by Republicans.

The full text of the letter can be found below or here:

Dear Secretary Mullin:

We write in strong opposition to the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) recent waivers of numerous federal environmental and historic preservation laws inside Big Bend National Park. These waivers endanger the intrinsic nature of the park, local economies, biodiversity, and the safety of communities along the Rio Grande River. We urge you to rescind these waivers and instead offer proposals subject to public review and input. There is no border security emergency here that warrants giving CBP unfettered authority to unnecessarily destroy some of the wildest parts of Big Bend or to disregard the overwhelmingly bipartisan will of the people, the actual data showing minimal numbers of border crossings inside the park, and the values that Texans and all Americans hold dear as represented by the National Parks.

The administration has failed to demonstrate that Big Bend National Park is an area of high illegal entry–a requirement under Section 102(c) of the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act of 1196, as amended (IIRIRA). Your notice of the waivers does not contextualize the number of illegal entry incidents. In Fiscal Year 2025 (FY25), Big Bend Sector recorded 0.45% of all illegal border crossings nationwide. Big Bend Sector represents the lowest level of illegal activity along the entire border, with the National Park itself comprising even fewer instances, disqualifying the region from your claims of high activity. The rough terrain of Big Bend itself and Mexican lands to the south form a natural wall deterring illegal activity with its rugged terrain, as CBP has acknowledged.

Sheriffs from the region have written to you that this proposed construction is unnecessary, especially given the successes of ongoing practices. Issuing these waivers bypasses all opportunity for stakeholder comment and ignores state and federal land managers, local law enforcement, and local residents who know the area best. We urge you to reverse these dangerous waivers and meaningfully engage with, and transparently respond to the input provided by, the National Park Service, local government, and the public.

title: Trump administration's immigration crackdown gives local jails a financial boost | Connecticut Public
description:
LEILA FADEL, HOST: Local jails can earn a lot of money for locking up people taken into custody by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.
LEWIS: Most all jails cost their local county taxpayers a lot of money.
WATKINS: ICE used local jails under past presidents, too.
WATKINS: Navarrete was locked up for more than three months before a federal judge ordered her release in November.
Data show ICE has sent more than 6,000 immigrants just to Kentucky jails under Trump.
text:
LEILA FADEL, HOST:

Local jails can earn a lot of money for locking up people taken into custody by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement. More than 100 jails across the country have done this in President Trump's second term. Morgan Watkins with the Kentucky Center for Investigative Reporting looks at how the arrangement works in her state.

MIKE LEWIS: Control, open 202 - two, zero, two.

(SOUNDBITE OF DOOR CLICKING)

MORGAN WATKINS, BYLINE: Mike Lewis walks down the hallway in the jail he runs in rural Hopkins County, Kentucky. The lights are dim. The walls are gray. He stops at a pair of large windows. On the other side, over a dozen detainees in striped uniforms, mostly all Hispanic, sit around.

LEWIS: Watching TV and playing cards and waiting for dinner to be served. Like I said, we usually feed them right at 12 o'clock. So about five or 10 minutes, trays will be rolling back.

WATKINS: These men are immigrants. They were arrested by ICE because they were in the country illegally and sent to Lewis' jail. Many will probably be deported.

LEWIS: They're the easiest inmates in the building to deal with. Their cells are always the cleanest. They hardly ever fight amongst themselves. They are hardly ever disrespectful to our staff.

WATKINS: The federal government pays a fee for each day a jail holds someone for ICE. The amount is negotiated with each facility and varies widely. In Kentucky, public records show some jails getting paid between $45 and $100 per person a day. Lewis says the arrangement can offset expenses, fill empty beds and keep the jail busy enough that they don't have to lay off staff.

LEWIS: Most all jails cost their local county taxpayers a lot of money. The goal is to cost as little as possible. That's my goal for the county.

WATKINS: ICE used local jails under past presidents, too. But the Trump administration in particular has sought more space to incarcerate immigrants because it has been arresting a lot more of them. ICE says it's a top priority to ensure the well-being of people in its custody. And the agency says that it has high standards for detention. However, recent lawsuits allege people experienced inhumane conditions and inadequate care while in ICE custody. People in some communities are fighting their local jail's decision to work with ICE. Alex LeBlanc leads a group of citizens in Oldham County, Kentucky. They've protested at county meetings and outside the jail.

ALEX LEBLANC: It's sanctioned human trafficking by the American government, and they're funding it, and they're incentivizing it. And that's pretty gross.

WATKINS: LeBlanc and other residents say their local elected officials shouldn't put revenue over people, people like Leyla Navarrete. She's in her late 20s, from Nicaragua and now lives in Indiana. Federal agents arrested Navarrete last year when she arrived for an appointment at an immigration office in Indianapolis.

LEYLA NAVARRETE: (Through interpreter) So I was in shock. I couldn't believe. It was like a dream. It was very - I couldn't believe. It was a surprise. And I was - all the time was thinking, like, what I did wrong?

WATKINS: ICE sent Navarrete to Kentucky's Grayson County Detention Center. She was pregnant, in her second trimester. She said she felt like a criminal during a checkup when jail staff took her to a local doctor.

NAVARRETE: (Through interpreter) At the appointment, I started crying and crying because it was my first baby and I wanted the dad to be there, my husband. The doctor then touched my shoulder and said that everything would be fine. And I felt that there was still some humane people, good people.

WATKINS: Navarrete was locked up for more than three months before a federal judge ordered her release in November. The jail was able to charge the U.S. government for every day that she was in there. Data show ICE has sent more than 6,000 immigrants just to Kentucky jails under Trump. Four of those jails billed ICE for over $2 million each so far.

For NPR News, I'm Morgan Watkins in Louisville.

(SOUNDBITE OF NATHAN SALSBURG'S "IMPOSSIBLE AIR") Transcript provided by NPR, Copyright NPR.

By: Gladys Gervacio | June 16, 2026

Overview

In a significant development regarding the controversial $100,000 H-1B supplemental fee, the United States District Court for the District of Massachusetts has temporarily stayed the effect of its earlier ruling that vacated the fee requirement. As a result, the $100,000 fee remains in effect while appellate proceedings move forward.

Background

On June 8, 2026, the District Court in State of California et al. v. Noem et al. ruled that the federal government's implementation of the $100,000 H-1B fee was unlawful. The court found that the fee constituted an unauthorized tax that exceeded executive authority, infringed upon Congress's taxing power, and violated the Administrative Procedure Act (APA).

The court vacated the policies and agency guidance that implemented the fee, which, if allowed to take effect, would have prohibited U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) and the Department of State from collecting the fee nationwide.

Following the decision, the federal government promptly filed a notice of appeal with the U.S. Court of Appeals for the First Circuit and sought emergency relief to prevent disruption while the appeal is pending.

Administrative Stay Granted

On June 12, 2026, the District Court denied the government's request for a stay based on the merits of the case but granted an administrative stay pending further review by the First Circuit Court of Appeals.

The administrative stay temporarily suspends the effect of the June 8 ruling and allows the government to continue collecting the $100,000 H-1B fee while the appellate court considers the government's motion for a stay pending appeal.

As a result, the $100,000 H-1B supplemental fee currently remains in effect and must continue to be paid where required.

The First Circuit is expected to determine whether a longer-term stay should remain in place during the appeal process.

Practical Implications for Employers

Employers sponsoring H-1B workers should be aware of the following:

The $100,000 H-1B supplemental fee remains enforceable at this time.

USCIS and the Department of State may continue collecting the fee while the administrative stay is in effect.

The legal status of the fee remains uncertain and could change quickly depending on future rulings by the First Circuit Court of Appeals.

Employers with pending or planned H-1B filings should closely monitor developments and consult immigration counsel regarding case-specific filing strategies.

What Employers Should Do Now

Until further guidance is issued:

Continue to assume that the $100,000 H-1B fee applies to covered cases.

Coordinate filing timelines and budgets accordingly.

Monitor court developments closely, as the status of the fee may change on short notice.

Consult with immigration counsel regarding any pending, planned, or time-sensitive H-1B filings.

description:

text:
Fifteen people in Minnesota were charged with conspiracy to impede or injure federal officers over their response to a controversial and deadly immigration enforcement crackdown in the state earlier this year.

The US attorney for Minnesota, Daniel Rosen, and the special agent in charge of Homeland Security Investigations for Minnesota, Michael McCarthy, announced the charges at a press conference in Minneapolis on Tuesday.

The prosecutors allege the defendants were part of two Minneapolis-based “antifa” groups that “violently oppose immigration law enforcement”. The indictment names the two groups as Direct Action Minnesota and Black Cat Worker’s Collective, which it described as a subgroup.

Of those charged, 12 people were arrested on Tuesday and one was already in custody on other federal charges, according to officials, who said two remain at large.

Chaotic scenes erupted outside the federal courthouse in Minneapolis on Tuesday, where some of the defendants made their first appearance on Tuesday. Protesters clashed with federal agents, who deployed teargas and pepper spray as they tried to disperse the crowd, according to video footage and witnesses.

Earlier in the afternoon, a group of dozens of people gathered to speak out against the charges, including Nekima Levy Armstrong, who was charged in a separate case involving a protest at a church. Signs among the crowd carried messages such as “stop FBI entrapment” and “protesting is not a crime”.

The new charges come as other cases from the federal government against protesters have fallen apart. The US attorney’s office’s track record with charges filed related to the crackdown, which was known as “Operation Metro Surge”, was the subject of media questions during the press conference. MPR News noted that the office has so far dropped 18 of its 36 prior cases, including one where a judge called a charging document a “false affidavit”.

With these new charges, Rosen said, “the evidence will prove it all out”.

Rosen showed social media posts and videos of a couple of the people indicted to underscore the allegations that they intended to impede law enforcement. In one video, a man declares he is antifa and discusses bringing guns to a demonstration. He showed another post of a defendant saying people needed to “become ungovernable”.

Antifa, which is short for “antifascist”, is not a specific group, but rather a decentralized movement, but last fall, the Trump administration categorized “antifa” as a “domestic terror organization”. Rosen did not define what “antifa” was, saying it went “beyond the scope” of today’s indictment.

At the demonstration, Bruce Nestor, a former president of the National Lawyers Guild, spoke to the crowd, saying: “What’s wrong with being ungovernable?” Nestor described the charges as “thought crimes” and an “act of political retribution” designed to quell dissent.

Rosen did not answer repeated questions about whether any agents or officers were injured by the defendants. The indictment does not allege officers were injured, though it mentions kicking a federal vehicle and knocking notes from an agent’s hands.

“Whether or not they actually at the end of the day caused bodily harm is not the measure of whether or not they committed a serious crime,” he said.

The Trump administration sent in thousands of immigration agents to Minnesota starting in late 2025, in part predicated on fraud allegations against Somali residents. The crackdown led to protest and a broad community response, from people monitoring agents to providing food for those staying home. Agents killed two people – Renee Good and Alex Pretti – in the streets, leading to further protest.

The agents who killed Good and Pretti have not faced charges. Rosen said during the press conference that the killings were under investigation, and charges could be possible.

The charges are the latest attempt by federal prosecutors to crack down on opposition to immigration enforcement.

Rosen also alluded that there could be more charges as they continue investigating response to the Minnesota crackdown. “If you are actively conspiring to impede law enforcement … you ought to go on the assumption that we’re watching, and we’ll get you,” he said.

The indictment mentions rapid response networks, which came together to track immigration agents’ vehicles as they were arresting people around the state. It also discusses how defendants used the encrypted chat app Signal to coordinate among people who were monitoring activity by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents. Rosen called these tactics “stalking” and noted how one of the defendants followed an agent from the federal building in St Paul to western Wisconsin.

It cites activities at the federal Whipple building in St Paul, where immigration agents were headquartered, saying the defendants set up “hard” and “soft” blockades to impede agents’ abilities to do their jobs. These hard blockades consisted of debris, vehicles or physical items, while soft blockades included people lined up with shields.

Earlier this year, the Trump administration secured its first successful conviction on the basis of “antifa” terrorism in the Prairieland case in north Texas, following a non-fatal shooting at a 4 July 2025 noise demonstration, in a case with 22 defendants across federal and state charges.

The Minnesota defendants do not currently face terrorism charges. Rosen said the indictment filed on Tuesday reflected charges that the office has the evidence to convict over.

In Spokane, Washington, three activists were convicted of conspiracy charges over an anti-ICE demonstration. The federal government also charged six people in Illinois with conspiracy over a protest at the Broadview detention facility, though the government later dropped the charges amid claims of prosecutorial misconduct.

Kat Abughazaleh, one of the six charged at Broadview, noted on Bluesky that the Minneapolis charges mirror the ones she faced.

“We need to be asking how they got this indictment. And as charges (hopefully) get dropped, we must remember the process is the punishment,” she said.

A federal judge refused to throw out former Milwaukee County Judge Hannah Dugan's conviction for interfering with an ICE arrest. U.S. District Judge Lynn Adelman issued the ruling June 16 in Milwaukee.

Dugan was found guilty by a jury of obstructing ICE's arrest of Eduardo Flores-Ruiz at a Milwaukee courthouse on April 18, 2025.

Advertisement

Agents had investigated Flores-Ruiz's immigration status, confirmed he had been deported in 2013 and returned to the country without permission, and obtained a warrant for his arrest before trying to take him into custody.

After trial, Dugan asked Adelman to reconsider based on a recent appeals court decision from Virginia. In that case, United States v. Hernandez, a divided panel of the Fourth Circuit ruled that ICE's attempt to carry out a deportation order did not qualify as a "pending proceeding" under the federal obstruction statute.

Adelman said the two cases were different. In Hernandez, an immigration court had already ordered the defendant deported, and ICE was simply trying to put him on a plane when he escaped custody.

In Dugan's case, ICE was still in the middle of its own process — investigating Flores-Ruiz, obtaining a warrant, and preparing to determine whether his earlier deportation order should be reinstated.

"Unlike in Hernandez, at the time of the obstructive conduct in this case there was no final order of removal," Adelman wrote.

The judge also rejected the broader argument that ICE enforcement actions can never be covered by the obstruction statute. He pointed to rulings from the Seventh and Ninth circuits holding that the SEC's enforcement of securities laws and the IRS's collection of tax debts both qualified as agency proceedings protected by the statute.

Adelman noted that ICE is different from agencies like the FBI because it can issue its own warrants and make its own removal decisions without going through a court, putting its work in a different category than routine police activity.

Prosecutors also argued that ICE had an additional purpose beyond the arrest: determining whether Flores-Ruiz should face criminal charges for illegal reentry. That referral was made, and he was charged.

Flores-Ruiz was deported Nov. 13, 2025. Dugan's case will move to sentencing.

WASHINGTON, D.C. – Today, Congressman Rob Menendez demanded a stop to third country deportations to the Democratic Republic of the Congo (“DRC”) and other countries by the Trump Administration. Menendez called on Department of Homeland Security (“DHS”) Secretary Markwayne Mullin and Immigration and Customs Enforcement (“ICE”) Senior Officer David Venturella to halt this practice, provide assurances no further removals will take place to countries where DHS later claims they cannot retrieve deported individuals from, and to stop the use of third country deportations to further President Trump’s mass deportation agenda.

The effort follows the Trump Administration’s deportation of Adriana Quiroz Zapata, Congressman Menendez’s constituent and a Colombian native protected under the Convention Against Torture, to the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

In the letter, Menendez stated:

“It is both morally and logistically indefensible to forcibly remove individuals to countries from which the Administration is unwilling to return them, even when such return is ordered by the courts. I urge DHS to immediately suspend any plans to deport individuals to the DRC or to any third country destination that the Administration claims is not operationally viable for returns, including those affected by public health emergencies such as Ebola outbreaks.”

“I have seen the consequences of these illegal practices firsthand. My constituent, Adriana Zapata, was deported to the DRC in violation of the law and the Congolese government’s documented refusal. Since her forcible removal to a country that is unable to provide baseline humanitarian protections, Adriana has faced arbitrary detention, medical deterioration, and continued pressure from Congolese and Colombian officials to relinquish her Convention Against Torture protections and agree to refoulement to Colombia,” Menendez continued.

“If the Trump Administration truly considers conditions in certain countries so severe as to preclude safe return, it cannot simultaneously argue that deporting our community members to those same countries is safe or justified. DHS must halt any such removals immediately, provide clear assurances that no one will be removed to locations from which the Trump Administration claims safe return is not possible, and cease the use of third country deportations to further the President’s mass deportation agenda. The Trump Administration bears responsibility for the harms Adriana and other removed individuals continue to endure in the DRC and other third countries. I urge you to promptly address this urgent matter, and I look forward to your response,” Menendez concluded.

Menendez is demanding that DHS and ICE:

Halt third country removals to countries where DHS and ICE claim to not be able to facilitate a safe return in response to court orders;

Provide clear assurances that no one will be removed to location where the Trump Administration claims safe return is not possible; and

Cease the use of third country deportations to further President Trump’s deportation agenda.

Since coming to Congress, Rob Menendez has been a leader on fighting for immigrant rights. Menendez has fought to facilitate the return of Adriana Quiroz Zapata for over a year, and attended a court hearing in her case in Washington, D.C. after her wrongful deportation.

text:
Since school let out for her 5-year-old son last month, Maria Celeste spends her days pinching pennies and tending to her two children, Ian and Alice, all by herself. Things would’ve been a lot different had her fiancé — who, according to the United States government, entered the county without legal authorization — just heeded the flashing warning signs last fall and stayed home rather than driving into work.

“We had been told that Border Patrol was doing a lot of checkpoints on that street,” she said about the stretch of I-10 entering Mississippi from Louisiana.

Maria Celeste — who is also an immigrant seeking asylum in the U.S. — requested that she be identified only by her first and middle names. She asked that Verite News not reveal her or her children’s last names or her country of origin because she has an open asylum claim, and she’s afraid of being targeted, separated from her kids or subjecting them to detention themselves.

On that stormy September morning when her fiancé, Antony, was arrested, Maria Celeste lay in bed recovering from a C-section she had some three weeks prior, giving birth to Alice. Antony was on his way to Mississippi from their home in southeast Louisiana, despite hearing from colleagues that the U.S. Border Patrol was active along I-10.

The couple did not comprehend the risk Antony was taking. He had filed an asylum claim with the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services earlier last year and, according to Maria Celeste, believed he was safe from arrest while the legal process was playing out. They agreed that if he got pulled over, he could simply show his court paperwork and would be allowed to go on with his day.

He told her he would call home when he arrived safely at work. But the phone call never happened. Instead, the Border Patrol pulled him over, arrested him and handed him over to U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

Today, Antony, a 28-year-old Honduran citizen, is incarcerated in one of the nation’s largest immigration detention centers, Adams County Correctional Center, a facility that sits on 14 acres of land near Natchez, Mississippi. He asked that his last name not be published out of fear of retaliation from guards at the facility, from ICE or from people in Honduras should he have to return. Adams, which is owned and run by CoreCivic, one of the country’s largest private prison operators, can house more than 2,000 people.

Antony is one of hundreds of immigrants locked up in Adams who have filed habeas corpus claims against the Trump administration, challenging their ongoing detention as illegal. In his petition, Antony is arguing that he is eligible for an immigration bond hearing and not getting one violates his right to due process.

At Adams Correctional, Antony said he’s severely depressed from the isolation from his family. It’s taken a physical and emotional toll, he said in an interview with Verite News, and he’s concerned about a potential skin cancer diagnosis.

At home, Maria Celeste is carrying multiple stressors alone. She’s taking care of a newborn baby, the finances are strained, she needs surgery for her back to fix a spinal problem, and her son, recently diagnosed with autism, has had trouble coping since his father was taken by ICE.

During the second Trump administration, the number of people challenging immigration detention in the country has been historically high, clogging up the courts. The cases can often take months or more to resolve, while Antony and others like him are stuck in detention.

To try and move things along, Maria Celeste requested in April that Antony’s attorneys file a motion to expedite Antony’s habeas case, which has seen no movement since March. Antony also has another case before the Board of Immigration Appeals. After he was detained, a judge dismissed his asylum case without granting him a final hearing, and he’s appealing that decision.

Maria Celeste said the couple is now having tough conversations about what to do next. With no end in sight in the legal process, they are considering having Antony leave for Honduras voluntarily. While he languishes in detention, struggling with his own physical and mental health amid what he describes are difficult conditions, the couple is discussing Antony possibly opting for deportation to bring their ordeal to a resolution.

“If the decision ends up being negative,” Maria Celeste said about their requested motion to expedite, “we may withdraw the appeal and have Antony return to Honduras. As heartbreaking as that is, he cannot continue waiting indefinitely inside Adams under these conditions.”

Detained at a traffic stop

According to court documents, Antony came to the U.S. in late 2021, entering the country without presenting himself to federal authorities at the border. In his asylum application, he said he left Honduras fleeing organized crime, fearing that his life was in danger. Antony’s attorneys have argued that he’s a good candidate to be allowed to stay in the U.S. He has no criminal record, no history of violence and he supports himself. After arriving, he started his own business doing construction, painting and repair work.

His dream in coming to the U.S., he said, was to work, go to church, and spend time with family.

The couple first met before Antony came to live in the U.S. and have been engaged since 2024. Before Antony’s arrest, they had planned to marry this past January. She said both of them were thrilled to have just brought a new baby girl into the world.

All of that fell apart when he was taken by the U.S. Border Patrol in September.

On September 25, 2025, Antony woke up early to drop Maria Celeste’s mother off for a flight at the New Orleans International Airport. She had been visiting for the birth of her granddaughter and was heading back overseas. After dropping her off, he took I-10 going eastbound from Jefferson Parish to get to a job site in Mississippi. According to Antony, he drove into Mississippi, and it was right at Exit 2 where he was pulled over by Border Patrol.

Maria Celeste remembers waking up around 6:30 a.m. to Antony’s phone call. She remembers him saying an unmarked car flashed its patrol lights, and pulled him over. She remembers a Border Patrol agent was asking him where he’s going and if he’s a citizen. Both of them thought at the time that they should respond openly to the questions of law enforcement, because, Maria Celeste said, they believed having an open case and having no criminal record would insulate them from the worst case scenario — arrest, detention and family separation.

“Now, if this were to happen to him, he wouldn’t have shared any information. He would have said, ‘I want to remain silent and talk to my lawyer,’” Maria Celeste said.

A U.S. Customs and Border Protection spokesperson did not address details about the encounter like whether Antony shared his pending asylum case with the arresting officer, but the spokesperson confirmed by email that Border Patrol arrested Antony in Mississippi and handed him over to ICE.

“Pending immigration benefit requests do not preclude enforcement of federal immigration law, including immigration detention,” the spokesperson said.

After questioning him, according to Maria Celeste, they took his phone, hung up the call and she broke down in tears.

“I just started to cry and yell, and I just grabbed my baby, and I got in my car,” she said.

Maria Celeste raced to the airport trying to reach her mom before her mom could board the flight, because she didn’t know what else to do, she said. She was still dizzy every time she stood up, a reaction she had experienced since the surgery. She remembers thinking that she would need help retrieving Antony’s car, and her son kept asking where his dad was.

“I could only really cry because I didn’t really know how to explain to him or how to answer his questions,” she said.

During an interview in April, Maria Celeste shared a photo album of Ian’s most recent birthday, the only birthday Antony ever missed, she said. Ian, who like his little sister was born in the U.S., was turning five. At the time, Antony had been in detention for just over a month, mainly at the Central Louisiana ICE Processing Center in Jena, Louisiana. He was moved into Adams in February, Maria Celeste said.

Maria Celeste turned the page of the photo album to show the only picture that she has of Antony with his daughter. Alice was just over three weeks old when he was arrested.

“It’s really unfortunate that he’s not able to be with her right now,” she said.

‘I have deteriorated both physically and mentally’

Today, Antony is approaching nine months in immigration detention. Lengthier periods of detention have become more common during the second Trump administration. In part, that is because the administration has sought, and succeeded in some cases, to change the rules to favor detention over monitored release.

Last year, for example, ICE rewrote a longstanding policy that previously allowed immigrants who were arrested in the interior of the country, rather than at the border, to pursue bond hearings in immigration court. Under the rewritten policy, those immigrants would be treated the same as new arrivals — no matter how long they had been in the country — making them ineligible for bond. Earlier this year, the new policy was affirmed by the U.S. 5th Circuit Court of Appeals, which has jurisdiction over Texas, Louisiana and Mississippi.

With release on bond mostly off the table, the only option many people in immigration detention have to seek relief from incarceration is to file a habeas petition, a legal action, by which someone can challenge the lawfulness of their detention. The U.S. Supreme Court case Zadyvdas v. Davis established a six-month threshold, after which ongoing detention can be challenged as illegal.

Nora Ahmed, legal director of the ACLU of Louisiana, said that the Zadvydas decision clarifies that the government cannot use immigration detention as a form of punishment.

But Ahmed said she worried that because there’s pressure from the administration to keep deportation numbers high and that incarceration is a means to coerce people to voluntarily give up their rights and return to their countries of origin.

“It seems to be in order to punish them for even having come to the country, and to ultimately make them self-deport,” she said.

Maria Celeste said that is exactly what has happened to Antony and why they’re now considering self-deportation for Antony. They’re concerned about Antony’s physical and mental health with what seems to them to be no end in sight for his detention.

“I feel terrible and deeply depressed, as I have deteriorated both physically and mentally,” Antony said.

For Antony, who describes conditions in detention as so difficult that he’s lost hope, it’s not just being separated from his family that makes him feel bad, but he also said that he believes the quality of the food and the hygiene standards have caused him to have stomach issues. He said for the stomach issues he has been given an antacid that doesn’t help him, so he ends up avoiding certain foods. Antony said that he’s lost 40 pounds in detention.

“I really just want to get out, and I want to get back to work, and I just want to keep fighting for a happy life for my family, and I want to have the ability to share in [their] happiness and teach my children the things they need their dad for,” Antony said.

Maria Celeste said that Antony was also worried about a dark spot on his face. According to her, his family has a history of cancer and the couple wanted to get the mark checked out before he was detained. She’s worried that Adams County Correctional Center lacks appropriate medical care to help him.

Ryan Gustin, a spokesperson for CoreCivic, the private prison company that operates Adams County Correctional Center as one of its many ICE-contracted facilities, addressed food and medical concerns in an email. Gustin said that CoreCivic’s top priority is the “safety, health and well-being of the individuals entrusted to our care.”

Gustin said that the detention center provides three nutritious meals a day and takes great care to offer meals that support specialized diets.

“Many of our employees eat these same meals at the facility,”

In terms of appropriate and timely medical care, Gustin added that everyone detained at Adams has access to sign up for medical care daily, and that the facility has a clinic staffed with licensed healthcare professionals. The company ensures access to off-site care for residents, including a referral to a dermatologist, if deemed appropriate.

“We take seriously our obligation to adhere to all applicable federal detention standards and will continue to ensure that all detainees receive appropriate and timely medical attention.”

A Department of Homeland Security spokesperson said medical staff at the center evaluated Antony after a walk-in request earlier this month to be checked for skin cancer, and the staff noted he had a few small pimples that appeared to be irritated from scratching. The center prescribed him an antiseptic gel to apply to the affected area, did not refer him to an outside medical provider and instructed him to return if needed, the DHS spokesperson said.

But Maria Celeste said she’s not confident they’ve been taking his concerns seriously. According to Maria Celeste, he’s asked multiple times in the past to be seen, and the irritated pimples are different from the longstanding mark on his face. She said she believes media attention prompted the center to start addressing his medical complaints more seriously.

“The concern has never been a few irritated marks,” she said. “The concern is the darker spot that Antony has had for a long time and that he was planning to have medically evaluated before he was detained.”

She said she wishes more Americans knew two things about immigration detention. First, Maria Celeste wishes more people were aware about the criminal statistics of people in immigration detention.

The most recent information from data research organization Transactional Records Access Clearing House (TRAC) at Syracuse University shows that the vast majority (more than 70%) of people in ICE detention have no criminal record. An ABC News analysis found that only 3% of the people detained by ICE over the first 14 after Trump came into office had a violent felony conviction. And at the end of March, Mississippi Today found that only 9% of people in Adams have any sort of criminal conviction.

She also wishes more people could see the detention conditions, including the food and the medical care that people in prolonged detention are subject to. She thinks if more people got a more transparent look behind the closed doors of detention centers like Adams, the public would be asking a lot more questions.

Gustin said the facility is monitored closely by ICE, undergoes regular review and audit processes and is visited by elected officials, immigration attorneys and others.

‘Sometimes people just need someone who understands’

At home with the kids, Maria Celeste said she spends her days taking care of the house by herself and trying to spend quality time with her two children. One of her vertebrae has slipped out of alignment, along with a few other spinal injuries that cause her pain when doing certain activities that put pressure on her back, some of them like bending down, unavoidable for a new mother. Antony was the sole financial provider for the household before he was detained.

Since Antony’s incident, Ian, the couple’s five-year-old son, has been diagnosed with adjustment disorder and autism, he has suffered chronic migraines and has had nightmares and trouble sleeping, Maria Celeste said, providing doctors’ diagnoses for review. A doctor’s notes she provided described the importance of family stability for conditions like autism. Maria Celeste ascribes the onset of these issues directly to Antony’s sudden departure.

In the free time she has, Maria Celeste has formed a small network of friends in similar circumstances who share stories and legal advice and monitor court decisions that can have an impact on broader immigration policy. She said that her group of friends formed out of necessity. Since mass deportation began, Maria Celeste said she’s seen wives, mothers, children, churches and even strangers helping each other find information, locate loved ones, raise money, find attorneys and bond together to survive emotionally.

“Now,” she said, “I find myself doing for others what others once did for me. Sometimes people just need someone who understands what they are going through.”

Antony, in his desperation for relief, described his fate as up to God.

“I am leaving everything in God’s hands,” he said, “[trusting] him to help me.”
